title: Consumer protection
examples: What are the main rights consumers have when buying things?
If I buy something broken, what can I do?
Who protects people who buy goods and services?

explain.say: Today we are learning about consumer protection rights.

items: Right to Safety: Goods must not harm you.
Right to Information: You need to know what you buy.
Right to Choose: You must have options available.

explain.say: The right to safety means products must not be dangerous to use.
The right to information means sellers must tell you all the facts.
The right to choose means you should not be forced to buy one thing.
If a product is faulty, you have the right to redress or a remedy.

draw.text: Redress: Getting a fix for problems.

explain.say: Imagine buying a toaster that only toasts one side of bread.

items: Toaster only toasts one side | Take it back | Get a refund

faq.q: What is the difference between consumer rights and consumer protection?
faq.a: Consumer rights are the basic rules that protect you as a buyer. Consumer protection refers to the laws and organizations that enforce those rights.
asks: Are rights and protection the same thing?

faq.q: If I am unhappy with a purchase, what is the first thing I should do?
faq.a: You should check the receipt and the product's warranty information. This helps you know your rights for returning it.
asks: How do I start a complaint?
Do I need a receipt to return something?

faq.q: Does the right to safety only cover electronics?
faq.a: No, it covers all goods and services. This includes food items and even things like cleaning chemicals.
asks: Is food covered by safety rights?

faq.q: What if the shop refuses to give me a refund?
faq.a: You can take the complaint to a local consumer advice centre or a relevant trading standards body.
asks: Who can help if a shop is unfair?
What if the shop owner is rude?

faq.q: Do I need to keep all the packaging when I return something?
faq.a: Yes, keeping the original packaging is usually important. It helps prove that the item was not damaged by you.
asks: Is the box important for returns?
Can I use a different box?

facts: Consumers have the right to be given correct information about goods.
If a product is dangerous, the right to safety is violated.
Redress means getting a remedy, like a refund or repair.
Consumer laws aim to make buying and selling fair for everyone.

quiz.say: A bottle of cleaning fluid leaks fumes that make you cough.
quiz.why: The fumes making you cough show the product is unsafe, which violates this right.

wrong.1: This right is about knowing ingredients, not about physical danger.
wrong.2: This right only relates to having multiple brands available.
wrong.3: Redress is what you do after the problem happens, not what describes the problem itself.

quiz.say: You buy a phone, but the seller tells you the battery lasts all day, but it only lasts four hours.
quiz.why: The seller giving false battery life information breaks your right to know the truth.

wrong.0: The battery life is a performance issue, not a physical danger.
wrong.1: This right concerns having options, not the accuracy of the description.
wrong.2: Redress is the solution you seek, not the problem itself.

quiz.say: You return a faulty jacket and the shop agrees to give you a brand new one.
quiz.why: Getting a replacement item is a form of remedy, which falls under redress.

wrong.1: The jacket was faulty, but the remedy is about fixing the transaction, not safety.
wrong.2: The problem was the fault, not a lack of information about it.
wrong.3: This right is about selection, not about fixing a damaged item.
